name: tag-dispatching
intent: Select the implementation of an operation at compile time from the type of a tag argument, so that generic code can vary behaviour per type property with no virtual dispatch and no runtime branch.
problem: Code that must behave differently for types sharing one signature but differing in a property the type system can express - an iterator's category, whether a type is trivially constructible, which numeric domain it belongs to. A dynamic decision (virtual call, type switch, enum field) costs a lookup, cannot be inlined, and demotes a static property to a runtime one.
context: Applies where the discriminating property is known at compile time and the set of implementations is either closed or deliberately extensible at compile time: standard-library algorithms selecting an O(1) or O(n) strategy from an iterator category, generic containers choosing trivial versus throwing construction, constructor disambiguation (range versus count, lock-adoption tags), and library extension points (serialization, hashing, formatting) that users must be able to extend for their own types without touching the dispatcher.
benefits: Zero runtime cost: the tag object is never read, stored or compared and is normally optimized away, so the selected path inlines like a direct call - no vtable, no indirect branch, no type check, no allocation.
A missing or wrong implementation is a compile-time problem, not a runtime type error, and every instantiated path is type-checked for its own types.

The tag is orthogonal to the payload: the same data can be routed to different implementations by changing only the tag, which is how std::vector carries both (count, value) and (first, last) construction.
Non-intrusive extension: tags are supplied by traits, type classes or marker implementations, so third-party and built-in types participate without being modified.
Open extension of the ladder: implementations can be added as new overloads in the user's own namespace (found by ADL) and are reached through the same public entry point.
Priority chains express 'use the most specific available implementation, otherwise fall back' with tag inheritance (or constraint subsumption) instead of SFINAE negation or nested conditionals.
tradeoffs: Silent fallback: if the overload for the most specific tag is missing, overload resolution promotes the argument to the nearest base tag and compiles a slower - or wrong - path without a diagnostic.

Diagnostics degrade: failures surface as 'no matching overload for tag type X' inside the ladder rather than as a message about the caller's type; concepts/requires and if constexpr produce far better messages.
Code size: every tag path multiplied by every instantiated type multiplies instantiations - the classic template-bloat bill for the zero-overhead gain, paid in compile time and binary size.
The tag set is closed, or at least centrally owned: a new property or a new priority level means touching the tag source (trait, instance) and the ladder.
Indirection in the source, not at runtime: the public function splits into a forwarding wrapper plus an implementation ladder, so a reader must jump once to find the algorithm that actually runs.

It is a compile-time mechanism only: anything that varies at runtime (configuration, user input, message contents) needs a runtime pattern such as a dispatch table or Strategy, and mixing the two forfeits the point.
Tests cannot substitute the selected implementation: each tag path must be instantiated explicitly, so per-path behaviour is covered only if the test names the tag.

participants.responsibility: An empty, behaviour-free type whose identity - never its value - encodes a capability, category or preference level; tags are related to one another (inheritance, ordering, constraint subsumption) so that specificity is ranked by the conversion sequence rather than by hand-written conditions.

Maps a client type to its tag: a member typedef, a trait specialization, an implicit/given instance or a marker type parameter; this is what keeps the mechanism non-intrusive for types that cannot be edited.
The single public entry point: obtains the tag for the caller's type, passes a value of that tag type (or supplies it as an implicit instance) and forwards to the ladder, so callers never name a tag.

One complete implementation per tag, kept in a detail or documented extension namespace and ordered by tag specificity; each overload carries a whole alternative algorithm, not a fragment of a branched one.
The concrete type whose property drives the choice; it only has to expose that property (a typedef, a trait specialization, a conformance, an instance) - it need not know that a ladder exists.

use_cases: Standard-library style algorithm selection: advance/distance taking a constant-time path for random-access iterators and a linear path otherwise, with no runtime branch.
Generic containers distinguishing trivial, nothrow and throwing construction of element ranges.
Constructor and factory disambiguation: ranges versus (count, value), std::adopt_lock/defer_lock/try_to_lock for locks, nothrow allocation.
Extension points where users supply implementations for their own types - serialization, hashing, formatting, comparison, transport adapters - through one public API with per-type behaviour.
Compile-time policy refinement: choosing the most specific implementation a type provides and falling back to a generic one through a priority chain.
Numeric and generic programming that must avoid runtime type inspection in hot loops while still accepting many types.

Boost.Iterator generalizes the std iterator-tag ladder into an orthogonal traversal hierarchy (no/incrementable/single_pass/forward/bidirectional/random_access_traversal_tag): iterator_traversal and iterator_category_to_traversal map an iterator to its tag and algorithms dispatch on the tag's convertible-to ranking instead of a fixed category enum.

LLVM's ADT headers: filter_iterator_impl is specialized on std::forward_iterator_tag versus std::bidirectional_iterator_tag and detail::fwd_or_bidi_tag derives the tag from the wrapped iterator, so make_filter_range gives bidirectional ranges operator-- while forward-only ranges compile just the forward path.

Julia's standard-library Val{x}: an empty parametric struct carries a constant into the type domain so methods like firstlast(::Val{true})/firstlast(::Val{false}) select without a runtime test - the idiom ported to a dynamic language, documented as paying off only when the value is a compile-time constant.
avoid_when: The decision depends on runtime data (configuration, user input, message contents): use a dispatch table, Strategy or a plain switch, all of which take values rather than types.

The toolchain is C++17 or newer and two branches in one function suffice: if constexpr is shorter, needs no tag types or helper overloads, and produces better errors; concepts cover constraint-based selection.
The type set is open and types arrive as runtime values: pay the virtual call (or a function table) instead of erasing types just to reach a compile-time ladder.

No one on the team is comfortable with overload ranking: the silent-fallback trap produces changes that look correct in review, whereas a virtual function or an enum switch is obvious to every reader.
The dispatch must cross a language or process boundary: the other side has no tag types, so a value tag plus a table is the honest mechanism.
anti_patterns: Tags that carry data: use behaviour-free tags for behaviour and strong types for data - splitting one value across several tag-like parameters hides the payload and makes the interface unreadable.

Bool tags at call sites with no semantics: construct(first, last, true_type{}) tells the reader nothing; name the tag after the decision (UseIteratorSemantics<true>) or the condition must be reconstructed from the implementation.
Levelling the ladder incompletely: a missing level silently promotes the tag to a base type, so the faster or intended path never runs and nothing warns.
Re-implementing if constexpr as a two-branch tag ladder in C++17+ code, or re-implementing a runtime switch as a template ladder for values that are only known at runtime.

Leaving the fallback overload constrained: the last level must accept any tag, otherwise types that fall through every higher level produce an avalanche of 'no matching overload' errors instead of one clear diagnostic.
Exposing the tag in the public API so that callers pass it explicitly everywhere: the mapping from type to tag has been dropped, and the tag has become a hand-maintained argument.
design_principles: Static polymorphism over dynamic polymorphism when the decision is known at compile time: no virtuals, no vtable, no indirect call, no type erasure.
Separation of interface and implementation: one public entry point hides a set of alternatively-compiled implementations.
Open/closed: new behaviour arrives as a new overload (or constraint) rather than as an edit to the dispatcher.
Non-intrusive extension: read type properties through traits or instances so that types which cannot be modified still participate (retroactive modelling).
Single responsibility per level: each tag path is a complete algorithm, which is why the levels can be instantiated independently.
Zero-overhead abstraction: the tag exists only to steer the compiler and must vanish from the generated code; if a mechanism costs at run time, the explicit runtime alternative is preferable.
best_practices: Keep exactly one public dispatch function; put the ladder in a detail namespace but leave it reachable (same namespace or ADL) so that it can be extended.
Encode priority in the types: derive tags from one another, or rely on constraint subsumption, so ranking is the type hierarchy rather than the argument order.
Always provide an unconstrained fallback level, and consider a deleted or static_assert-ed branch so that 'no implementation for this type' becomes one line of diagnostic.
Name tags after the decision they encode, never after the value, and give tag constants self-documenting names (std::defer_lock, std::nothrow) at the call site.
Take the tag from a trait or instance so that client types need not be modified; specialize the trait for third-party types instead of editing them.

On C++17+ first ask whether if constexpr (single function) or concepts (constraint-based selection) expresses the same intent with less machinery; keep tag dispatch for priority chains, separately-overloadable paths and open-world extension.
Count the instantiations when a ladder meets a combinatorial type space; template bloat and build time are the real bill for the zero-overhead dispatch.
Document the ladder's ordering: a reader must be able to see which level wins for a given tag without reasoning about conversion sequences.
